# Digital Cafe

2024-04-27

Welcome to Digital Cafe. This is the first installment of an introduction to web application programming. Our goal in this walkthrough is to teach you the very basics of how a "web application," as opposed to a mere "web page," works.

You can think of a web application (henceforth "web app") as a web page that stores data. This sounds like a simple addition, but it isn't. Having to manage data is where almost all the complexity of modern web development comes from. Thankfully, special programming libraries called _frameworks_ are available to help us design and run such applications easily.

In this walkthrough, we will be building a simple e-commerce application for a company that sells coffee. Users should be able to browse products, add products to their cart, and check out their orders. There are a lot of requirements in that one sentence.

We will use the Django framework to build our web app. The repository you are in right now is a snapshot of the code we had after writing documents 0001 through 0010. Note that you might not be able to download and run this repository directly, because we have excluded a settings file from the git repository. It shouldn't matter: you are meant to build Digital Cafe from scratch in your own repository. Use this repo as a guide, not as something to copy in its entirety.

## Objectives

After completing this walkthrough, you should be able to:

1. Build a simple web app from scratch using Django,
2. Reason about how to add a new feature to a Django web app.

We have adapted the official Django tutorial flow around the Digital Cafe web app concept instead of the Polls web app concept they use on their website.

It is beyond the scope of Digital Cafe to teach you about how "single-page apps" work. Django is excellent at producing so-called "multi-page apps", which reload the web browser every time you visit a new page. There is nothing wrong with sticking to this simple model as a beginner.

## Prework

### Installations

Bear with us, there is some setup that you need to do before running a Django project.

#### Mac

Please install the following on your computer:

- Python 3.11

Consider using Homebrew to install Python 3.11. Homebrew is a "package manager" that lets you install software from your terminal.

If you have Homebrew, run this command:

```zsh
brew install python@3.11
```

Refresh your shell:

```zsh
exec $SHELL
```

Verify that Python 3.11 has been installed:

```zsh
python3.11 --version
```

If you get a response with Python's version set to 3.11.x, you may proceed.

Make an empty directory and set it as your new working directory. This new directory will serve as the "root" of your entire Django project. We will call this directory `digitalcaferoot` for this tutorial.

```zsh
mkdir digitalcaferoot && cd digitalcaferoot
```

Make a Python virtual environment. This is where we will install our Python libraries.

```zsh
python3.11 -m venv env
source env/bin/activate
```

Your terminal prompt should now have a `(env)` prepended to it. This means that your `python` command now points to the virtual environment. Verify this by checking where `python` points to:

```zsh
which python
```

If you get a response pointing to a file inside the `env/` directory, you may proceed.

This is the last piece of setup for now. Install the `django` library.

```zsh
pip install django
```

Once this finishes, check if Django was installed:

```zsh
django-admin
```

If you get a help message, you may proceed.

#### Windows

Please install the following on your computer. You may get this software from Python's official website.

- Python 3.11

**Pay attention to the installer**. When it prompts you to "add Python to your PATH", tick the checkbox. If you missed this, open the installer again, uninstall Python, then reinstall Python with the checkbox ticked.

Open a PowerShell terminal. Check if Python 3.11 was installed properly by running:

```powershell
python --version
```

If you get a response with Python's version set to 3.11.x, you may proceed.

Make an empty directory and set it as your new working directory. This new directory will serve as the "root" of your entire Django project. We will call this directory `digitalcaferoot` for this tutorial.

```powershell
New-Item digitalcaferoot -ItemType Directory
Set-Location digitalcaferoot
```

Make a Python virtual environment. This is where we will install our Python libraries.

```powershell
python -m venv env
```

Since we are on Windows, there is a chance that we will need to allow external scripts to run. Open a new PowerShell window **as administrator** and run the following command:

```powershell
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser
```

Re-open a normal PowerShell window and navigate back to your `digitalcaferoot` directory. Now, you can activate your Python virtual environment:

```powershell
.\env\Scripts\activate.ps1
```

Your terminal prompt should now have a `(env)` prepended to it. This means that your `python` command now points to the virtual environment. Verify this by checking where `python` points to:

```powershell
Get-Command python
```
If you get a response pointing to a file inside the `env/` directory, you may proceed.

This is the last piece of setup for now. Install the `django` library.

```powershell
pip install django
```

Once this finishes, check if Django was installed:

```powershell
django-admin
```

If you get a help message, you may proceed.

### Theory

This part is optional, but highly helpful. A web app needs four parts to function:

- Routing HTTP requests based on their content and path ("routing")
- Storing data in a database and making it accessible to the rest of the app ("models")
- Rendering HTML based on data that may vary ("views")
- The glue logic between models and views ("controllers")

Web frameworks like Django (the framework we're using now), Flask, Ruby on Rails, and more all use these four basic concepts.

I wrote about these in this series of articles:

- https://joeilagan.com/article/2024-itm-web-apps-1
- https://joeilagan.com/article/2024-itm-web-apps-2
- https://joeilagan.com/article/2024-itm-web-apps-3

## Checkpoint

Please take a screenshot of your Terminal/PowerShell window after running the `django-admin` command.

# Hello Django

2024-04-28

In this section of the Digital Cafe walkthrough, we will set up your Django project.

The rest of this walkthrough assumes that you are familiar with your terminal or are at least capable of learning it. We will also be using UNIX file path conventions: directories and files will be separated by forward slashes (e.g., `digitalcaferoot/digitalcafe/manage.py`). Mac OS follows UNIX file path conventions. If you are on Windows, forward slashes are replaced by backward slashes (e.g., `digitalcaferoot\digitalcafe\manage.py`).

## Django development approach

The original version of Digital Cafe was written using Flask, which is a Python web microframework. This version of Digital Cafe is written using Django, which is a much heavier framework.

If you come across the Flask version of Digital Cafe, you may notice that it is structured as many quick iterations. This was only possible (and desirable) because Flask is not opinionated about how to handle web app development. In the Django version of Digital Cafe, we need to take things a little more slowly and thoroughly. In a similar, inverted way, this is only possible and desirable because Django already has the answers for building web apps.

For example, the Flask version of Digital Cafe starts by storing the database in a dictionary before iterating to MongoDB. We do not do this in Django because we only have one option for our database: a relational database. Yes, there are different flavors of relational database (SQLite vs. PostgreSQL, for instance), but the choice is made for us to use a relational database.

Being railroaded like this has its benefits. It makes it less mentally taxing to build features if you know that there's only one real way to do it.

## Structure of a Django project

A Django project is composed of multiple layers of directories, which each have multiple files.

The directory you created in the previous section, `digitalcaferoot`, is what we will call the "true root" of the entire Django project. It is the umbrella directory that contains every other file related to your Django project. Your true root will contain your Python virtual environment, and it is where you will start your Django editing sessions.

We will now create a Django project. Run this command in your terminal window. Make sure your virtual environment is active.

```bash
django-admin startproject digitalcafe
```

This will create a new directory called `digitalcafe`. We will call this directory the "project root."

You should now see this file structure, starting from the project root:

```
digitalcafe
├── digitalcafe
│   ├── asgi.py
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── settings.py
│   ├── urls.py
│   └── wsgi.py
└── manage.py
```

The top-level `digitalcafe` directory is the project root. The second-level `digitalcafe` is a _separate_ directory that we will call the "package directory." It contains more management files.

Let us briefly recap:

- There is a folder `digitalcaferoot` that is the "true root" of your entire Django project. It contains your Python virtual environment. When starting a coding session, you will usually start here and activate your virtual environment.
- There is a folder `digitalcaferoot/digitalcafe/` that is the "project root" of your Django project. It was created when you ran `django-admin startproject digitalcafe`. You will spend most of your terminal time here because it hosts `manage.py`, which is the file Django uses for command-line tasks.
- There is a folder `digitalcaferoot/digitalcafe/digitalcafe/` that is the "package directory" of your Django project.

Yes, it's confusing.

Thankfully, that's all we need to do to start your very first Django project. Navigate into the project root (i.e., `digitalcaferoot/digitalcafe/`) and run this command:

```bash
python manage.py runserver
```

Your terminal should display messages that it is now running a Django development server.

Open your web browser and navigate to the URL `http://localhost:8000`. This URL points to your local server; it can't be accessed by anyone else. You should now see a welcome page for Django, saying "The install worked successfully! Congratulations!"

## Checkpoint

Please take a screenshot of your browser, pointed at `http://localhost:8000`.

1 # Your first page 2 3 2024-04-28 4 5 We will now write your very first webpage with Django. There is a chance you have already done the "Intro to HTML" assignment. If you have not, or if your course doesn't have this assignment, in short: browsers render text formatted as Hypertext Markup Language (HTML). You can serve HTML as a file, or you can also serve it as a string from a web framework like Django. 6 7 ## Creating your webpage 8 9 There is a little more Django boilerplate we have to work through. Run this command to create a new "app." Django apps are sub-modules that Django uses to structure projects. Since we are only interested in making one web app, we will simply have a single Django app called "core." 10 11 ```bash 12 python manage.py startapp core 13 ``` 14 15 This will create a new app beside the package directory called `core/`. If you have followed the naming conventions so far, the full filepath of `core/` will be `digitalcaferoot/digitalcafe/core/`. 16 17 The `core/` directory will contain these files: 18 19 ``` 20 core 21 ├── admin.py 22 ├── apps.py 23 ├── __init__.py 24 ├── migrations 25 │ └── __init__.py 26 ├── models.py 27 ├── tests.py 28 └── views.py 29 ``` 30 31 We are primarily interested in the `core/views.py` file. Open it in your text editor. 32 33 Django routes HTTP requests to Python functions called "views." Views, being functions, can execute code. Ultimately, they must return something that the client can use, which usually means HTML. 34 35 In `core/views.py`, write the following code. Replace any code that may have been added by default. 36 37 ```python 38 from django.http import HttpResponse 39 40 def index(request): 41 return HttpResponse("Hello world!") 42 ``` 43 44 This function, `index`, is a view. We will now wire up this view to execute when you visit the server's root page, `/`. 45 46 Inside the `core/` directory, create a new file `core/urls.py`. Inside this file, write the following code: 47 48 ```python 49 from django.urls import path 50 51 from . import views # This . package just means "the current package; we are importing the sister file "views.py" 52 53 urlpatterns = [ 54 path("", views.index, name="index") 55 ] 56 ``` 57 58 We are not quite done. Go to the package directory (i.e., `digitalcaferoot/digitalcafe/digitalcafe/`) and modify `digitalcaferoot/digitalcafe/digitalcafe/urls.py` with the following code: 59 60 ```python 61 from django.contrib import admin 62 from django.urls import path 63 from django.urls import include # Add this line 64 65 urlpatterns = [ 66 path('admin/', admin.site.urls), 67 path("", include("core.urls")), # Add this line 68 ] 69 ``` 70 71 Yes, again, this is confusing. Every time you add a new view, you will need to register it with your app's `urls.py`, and every time you add a new app, you will need to register it with the package directory's `urls.py`. 72 73 Now your first view is ready. Run the server again and navigate to `http://localhost:8000/`. You should now see "Hello world!" rendered in your browser. 74 75 Remember that what you wrote in `core/urls.py` is text that can render HTML. If you want to try writing HTML instead of plain text, you can change the string from `"Hello world!"` to `"

Hello world!

"`. 76 77 ## Takeaways 78 79 I personally like to follow this workflow when adding a new view. 80 81 - First, write the function in your app's `views.py`. 82 - Then, register the function in your app's `urls.py`. 83 - Then, if necessary, register the whole app in your larger Django project's `urls.py`. 84 85 You may find out later on that Django supports something called "class-based views." We advise you to ignore this feature. Functions are much simpler and much easier to understand. 86 87 ## Checkpoint 88 89 Please screenshot your browser at `http://localhost:8000/`, displaying "Hello world!" as an _HTML header 1._ 90

1 # HTML 2 3 2024-04-28 4 5 You've seen how to write a basic view. Now, we will write a more complicated view to list the products available on our website. 6 7 ## The view as a function of data 8 9 Let's say that the Digital Cafe has only just opened. They only have two products: Americano, which is sold at PHP 110, and Cappuccino, which is sold at PHP 140. 10 11 You could easily write this as bare HTML, but one of the points of using a web framework is that the data that you must render will very likely change. It is generally unwise to write the data directly into your view like that. Most people choose to store their data somewhere then dynamically render the HTML based on the data. That's why we see the view as a _function_ of data: the view changes depending on the data. 12 13 ## Registering your app 14 15 Before we continue, we should register our `core` app with the larger Django package. Navigate to `digitalcafe/settings.py` and add this line to the `INSTALLED_APPS` list: 16 17 ```python 18 INSTALLED_APPS = [ 19 'core.apps.CoreConfig', # Add this line 20 'django.contrib.admin', 21 'django.contrib.auth', 22 'django.contrib.contenttypes', 23 'django.contrib.sessions', 24 'django.contrib.messages', 25 'django.contrib.staticfiles', 26 ] 27 ``` 28 29 This will tell Django that `core` is an active app. This step is necessary for the next section. 30 31 ## Templates 32 33 Let's modify the `index` view you made in the previous section to display the products instead of a hello world message. 34 35 ```python 36 def index(request): 37 products = [ 38 {"name": "Americano", "price": 110}, 39 {"name": "Cappuccino", "price": 140}, 40 ] 41 output = str(products) 42 return HttpResponse(output) 43 ``` 44 45 We now express our products first as data, then render them as a string. If you visit your index page now, you will see the products list, as a string, displayed on the web page. Of course, this is not what we intend: we want to format the products nicely. # The database

2024-04-28

We now come to one of the best parts of Django. As a framework, Django is incredibly good at managing a proper _database_ in which you can store your data. In this section, we will migrate our product data from a hardcoded list within the `index` view function to a proper database table in SQLite.

## Setting up the database

We haven't set up our database yet. Before we do anything related to the database, run this command.

```bash
python manage.py migrate
```

This tells Django to "migrate", or update, your database to a new state. Running this command for the first time tells Django to set up the database to its default state. The default migrations usually come from Django's built-in `admin` app, which we will use later.

You might see a new file, `digitalcaferoot/digitalcafe/db.sqlite3`. This is the SQLite database file that will store all of our app's data going forward. SQLite, of course, is not the only database engine we can use, but it is by far the easiest to set up, and it is more than capable of handling anything that a small website like Digital Cafe can throw at it.

## Making your own models

Let's now make our own database tables. We will start by making a table to hold data about our products. This means we need to create a model called `Product`, which will have at least two fields: a text field for the `name`, and a number field for the `price`.

Open `core/models.py` and add this code:

```python
from django.db import models

# Create your models here.

class Product(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=50)
    price = models.IntegerField()
```

Django models are represented as Python classes. When we eventually turn these models into database tables, each model will get its own database table.

We can now generate the migrations needed to transform our database to the state we prescribe in the `core/models.py` file by running this command.

```bash
python manage.py makemigrations core
```

Now that our migration files have been generated in `core/migrations/`, we can actually run the migrations by again running:

```bash
python manage.py migrate
```

The overall workflow of adding models is quite nice in Django. First, change `models.py`, then makemigrations, then migrate. Django helpfully figures out what changed between the last time you migrated, so you are free to specify what _end state_ you want your models to be in rather than be forced to write exactly how you want the database to change.

## Interacting with your models

Django models inherit from `models.Model`. This inheritance does a lot of heavy lifting. It gives Django models methods that make them very useful for create-read-update-delete (CRUD) operations.

We will test out our models in a Django shell. Open the Django shell with this command:

```bash
python manage.py shell
```

Import your models into the Django shell.

```python
>>> from core.models import Product
```

Now, you can perform CRUD on Products.

```python
>>> p = Product(name="Americano", price=110)
>>> p.save()
>>> p = Product(name="Cappuccino", price=130)
>>> p.save()
>>> Product.objects.all()
<QuerySet [<Product: Product object (1)>, <Product: Product object (2)>]>
>>> americano = Product.objects.get(name="Americano")
>>> americano.price
110
```

If you want to change the way a Product represents itself in code, you can provide an implementation for its built-in `__str__` method:

```python
class Product(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=50)
    price = models.IntegerField()
    def __str__(self):
        return f'{self.name}'
```

Now, if you open a new shell, you can see that Product is more human-friendly in the logs.

```python
>>> from core.models import Product
>>> Product.objects.all()
<QuerySet [<Product: Americano>, <Product: Cappuccino>]>
```

The takeaway here is that you can import models to be used in your views, too. This is how views can interact with your database. To make models available to views, import them like this:

```python
# In `core/views.py`
from .models import Product
```

## Checkpoint

Let's extend what you've learned in this section.

1. Add a new product, Espresso, whose price is PHP 100, to the database using the Django shell.
2. In your view function `index`, source your product data from the database instead of a hardcoded list.

Screenshot the Django shell, and screenshot your new code in `index`.

# The admin site

2024-04-28

In the previous section, we discussed how to design the database. The main issue with this is that anyone who wants to edit data would still need to know how to code. Most people in the world (and very likely your workplace) will not be technical, and they will also have a need to edit data in the backend.

Django provides an "admin" app by default to help your non-technical administrators change the database by themselves. We will set it up in this section.

## `createsuperuser`

Run this command to create a user account with administrator privileges. This type of account is typically called a "superuser" among software professionals.

```bash
python manage.py createsuperuser
```

You will be prompted for a username, an email, and a password. We will assume that you chose `cafeadmin` as your username.

Start the server and navigate to `http://localhost:8000/admin`. Here, you will be able to log in as the superuser you just created. Note, though, that your Product model from your `core` app will not be available. To make it available on the admin site, you will need to register the model in `core/admin.py`.

```python
from django.contrib import admin

from .models import Product

# Register your models here.

admin.site.register(Product)
```

Now, your admin site should make Product available to CRUD through a graphical interface.

Make a special note that the admin site's User model is also available for apps other than the admin app to use. In other words, you can simply use the registration/login functions freely provided by Django in `core`. We will make use of this later in the walkthrough. This is how Django apps are expected to manage users.

## Checkpoint

Screenshot yourself logged into your superuser account on the admin app.

Our next task is to let users click on a product on the main list and view a product detail page. 6 7 These next few pages will go fast. Our aim is to demonstrate that once you understand Django's basics, you can't help but move this fast. 8 9 ## Routing 10 11 We effectively want to have two main "pages." 12 13 - First, at `/`, a page to display the list of all products. We already have this page. 14 - Second, at `/product/`, a page to display the details of a specific product. Note that there is a variable part of this path, `product_id`. Django's routing helps us capture such variables. 15 16 When designing a website, you usually allow navigation between pages using _links_. The index page should link to each of the products, and the product pages should link back to the index. 17 18 ## Make a new view 19 20 We need to make a new view to handle the product page. We will follow the workflow for adding such a view. 21 22 Define a new function `product_detail` in your `core/views.py` file. Unlike `index`, it has to take an argument `product_id` due to the variable in the route that we plan to attach to it. For now, we will simply return the `product_id` variable to test if it works. 23 24 ```python 25 def product_detail(request, product_id): 26 return HttpResponse(str(product_id)) 27 ``` 28 29 Register your new view with `core/urls.py`. 30 31 ```python 32 urlpatterns = [ 33 path("", views.index, name="index"), 34 path("product/", views.product_detail, name="product_detail"), 35 ] 36 ``` 37 38 Note two things. First, the `name` parameter on each of these paths will be used as an identifier that we can use later in special helper functions. Second, in the first argument defining the path, enclose your variable and its data type in angle brackets. 39 40 Start the server. Navigate to `http://localhost:8000/product/1`. You should see the value "1" displayed on your web browser. This shows that your `product_detail` view function correctly captured the variable `product_id` as specified in `core/urls.py`. 41 42 ## Use the database 43 44 Of course, when we specify a product ID, we are not actually interested in the product ID itself but rather the product row that shares the ID. Our next task is to display the _name_ of the product instead of just the ID. 45 46 We can now use the Product model we set up in a previous section. If you have not already done so, import the Product model in `core/views.py`. 47 48 ```python 49 from .models import Product 50 ``` 51 52 Now, you can use the Product model in your view function. Let's simply render the name first without any HTML formatting to prove that we can do this. 53 54 ```python 55 def product_detail(request, product_id): 56 p = Product.objects.get(id=product_id) 57 return HttpResponse(str(p.name)) 58 ``` 59 60 When you visit `http://localhost:8000/product/1`, it should now render the name of the Product that has that ID (which is most likely "Americano"). 61 62 ## Link to the product pages 63 64 We are supposed to be able to directly visit the product pages from the index page. Revisit `core/templates/core/index.html`. If you have not already changed your `index` view function to use the database instead of the hardcoded list, replace it now with this code: 65 66 ```python 67 def index(request): 68 # Load the template 69 template = loader.get_template("core/index.html") 70 products = Product.objects.all() 71 context = { 72 "product_data": products 73 } 74 return HttpResponse(template.render(context, request)) 75 ``` 76 77 We now have access to the product ID. We can use that to create "anchor" tags in HTML, which are more commonly known to users as links. Let's assume that you have converted the HTML in `index.html` to render a table instead of an unordered list. 78 79 ```html 80 {% if product_data %} 81 82 83 84 85 86 {% for product_record in product_data %} 87 88 89 90 91 {% endfor %} 92
NamePrice
{{ product_record.name }}{{ product_record.price }}
93 {% endif %} 94 ``` 95 96 Inside this for loop, we can actually wrap the name inside an anchor tag as such. 97 98 ```html 99 {% if product_data %} 100 101 102 103 104 105 {% for product_record in product_data %} 106 107 108 109 110 {% endfor %} 111
NamePrice
{{ product_record.name }}{{ product_record.price }}
112 {% endif %} 113 ``` 114 115 It should be clear now how templating works. Anchor tags require you to specify a URL to which they point, and you can dynamically create those URLs using the data that you pass into a Django template. 116 117 Render your index page again. You should now see that the names of your products are hyperlinks. If you click on them, they should take you to the appropriate product page. 118 119 ## Using HTML for the product page 120 121 Now, we want to convert the product page from simply rendering the name of the product into a proper HTML page. We will follow the workflow for adding a new HTML template: 122 123 1. Create a new file, `core/templates/core/product_detail.html`. 124 2. We will pass in an instance of the Product model as context. Add HTML code that renders the product name and the product price. 125 3. Add an anchor tag that takes the user back to the main products page. 126 127 Here is an example of what you might have in your `product_detail.html` file. 128 129 ```html 130 Back to products 131 {% if product %} 132

Product name: {{ product.name }}

133

Product price: {{ product.price }}

134 {% endif %} 135 ``` 136 137 Convert your `product_detail` view to render this template. 138 139 ```python 140 def product_detail(request, product_id): 141 template = loader.get_template("core/product_detail.html") 142 p = Product.objects.get(id=product_id) 143 context = { 144 "product": p 145 } 146 return HttpResponse(template.render(context, request)) 147 ``` 148 149 This should have felt similar to what you did in `index`, and more importantly, it should have felt _correct_. Reload your browser page and play around with the website. Congratulations, you have added a new feature to your Django web app. 150 151 Do you remember the admin site from the previous section? If you add a Product to the database through that site, it will actually render on your main site. This is because you are now rendering the view as a function of what's in your database. This is how web apps become dynamic. 152 153 ## Checkpoint 154 155 Take two screenshots. The first screenshot should be of the index page (the page where all products are listed). The second screenshot should be of the Espresso page, assuming that you added Espresso to your products table in a previous section. 156

Name Price
{{ product_record.name }} {{ product_record.price }}

Name Price
{{ product_record.name }} {{ product_record.price }}

1 # The cart 2 3 2024-04-29 4 5 This is where all our Django experience now comes together. In this section, we will add the ability for users to add products to their cart. This feature will require us to touch almost every part of Django so far, from views to templates to models to routing. However, the hope is that it is crystal clear how Django helps you implement the feature. 6 7 ## Start with the model 8 9 Django becomes easier if you think of _everything_ as subordinate to the model. We should thus start here. 10 11 We only have two models right now: Product, which we made ourselves, and User, which we got out-of-the-box from Django. Pause to consider how you would model a shopping cart. Since this is a walkthrough, we will prescribe the model ourselves, but you should begin practicing data modeling now. 12 13 There will be one new model: CartItem. Each row of CartItem will represent one "line item" in the cart. A "line item" is a common concept in retail: it is composed of a product ID and a quantity. Together, many line items might make up a single transaction or, in this case, a single cart. 14 15 ```python 16 ... 17 from django.contrib.auth.models import User 18 ... 19 class CartItem(models.Model): 20 user = models.ForeignKey(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE, null=False) 21 product = models.ForeignKey(Product, on_delete=models.CASCADE, null=False) 22 quantity = models.IntegerField() 23 def __str__(self): 24 return f'{self.quantity} of {self.product} (User: {self.user.username})' 25 ``` 26 27 For now, we will assume that each User only has one Cart, but that the Cart may contain many CartItems. If you have taken a basic data modeling class, you should understand this intuitively. If you haven't taken a basic data modeling class, try [this](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xsg9BDiwiJE) video. 28 29 A CartItem is very much related to both the User who put the items in their cart and the Product that the user put into their cart. A CartItem should thus have _references_ to these other two tables. This is what _foreign keys_ are for. 30 31 We will now register our model. Remember these steps: 32 33 - Make migrations 34 - Migrate 35 - Add to admin site (if desired) 36 37 Since this is a walkthrough, here are the commands needed to execute these steps. 38 39 ```bash 40 python manage.py makemigrations core 41 python manage.py migrate 42 ``` 43 44 Then, in `core/admin.py`, add this code. 45 46 ```python 47 from .models import CartItem 48 admin.site.register(CartItem) 49 ``` 50 51 Now, superusers can use the admin site to manage CartItems. Of course, we want users to be able to manage their own CartItems. We will tackle this in the next subsection. 52 53 ## The user interface 54 55 How might a user add items to their cart? Never mind how a user might _want_ to do this; you can iterate on that later. For now, our only goal is to allow it at all. 56 57 It will be most straightforward for both us and the user to put another _form_ on each product detail page that lets a user specify a quantity to add to their cart. When the user clicks the form's submit button, the corresponding product and quantity should be added to their cart, and they should be redirected to the main index page. 58 59 We can achieve this in a similar way to how we built the login form. First, we can add a form to the product detail HTML template. 60 61 Change `core/templates/core/product_detail.html` to the following code. 62 63 ```html 64

Product details

65 Back to products 66 {% if product %} 67

Product name: {{ product.name }}

68

Product price: {{ product.price }}

69 {% endif %} 70 71

Add to cart

72
73 {% csrf_token %} 74 75 76 77 78
79 ``` 80 81 This form pattern should look very familiar. Note a little trick here. Since we want to add a CartItem, we will need both the quantity of the item to add and the ID of the item itself. We source the quantity from user input, but what about the product ID? We can add that ourselves by adding a "hidden" input field to our form with a pre-set value for the product ID. Now, the product ID will also be passed to the view when the form is submitted. 82 83 Of course, instead of sending its POST request to the login page, this form sends its post request to the `product_detail` view. We should now update this view to handle both GET requests for the normal page and POST requests for form submissions separately. 84 85 Update your code in the `product_detail` view to the following. 86 87 ```python 88 @login_required 89 def product_detail(request, product_id): 90 if request.method == 'GET': 91 template = loader.get_template("core/product_detail.html") 92 p = Product.objects.get(id=product_id) 93 context = { 94 "product": p 95 } 96 return HttpResponse(template.render(context, request)) 97 elif request.method == 'POST': 98 submitted_quantity = request.POST['quantity'] 99 submitted_product_id = request.POST['product_id'] 100 product = Product.objects.get(id=submitted_product_id) 101 user = request.user 102 cart_item = CartItem(user=user, product=product, quantity=submitted_quantity) 103 cart_item.save() 104 return redirect('index') 105 ``` 106 107 This code is brittle, but it works on the "happy path," which is when the user does what you originally expected them to do. There are a few edge cases that will break this code. For example, if a user adds multiple CartItems with the same product, the CartItems will not automatically get merged. You will have to handle that logic in the `product_detail` view if you want to rectify it. For the purposes of this walkthrough, we will ignore that edge case. 108 109 Note that when you are making a CartItem, the `user` and the `product` are supposed to be the objects themselves. That is why we have to fetch a product using the product ID first. 110 111 Let's add one last feature. When a user is redirected to the index, there should be a message telling them that they have added a CartItem to their cart. 112 113 Add this code somewhere in your `core/templates/core/index.html` file. 114 115 ```html 116 {% if messages %} 117
    118 {% for message in messages %} 119 {{ message }} 120 {% endfor %} 121
122 {% endif %} 123 ``` 124 125 Then, right after `cart_item.save()` in your `product_detail` file, add this code: 126 127 ```python 128 messages.add_message( 129 request, 130 messages.INFO, 131 f'Added {submitted_quantity} of {product.name} to your cart' 132 ) 133 ``` 134 135 Users of your app should now be able to add items to their cart. 136 137 ## Checkpoint 138 139 Take two screenshots: 140 141 - First, a screenshot of the Americano product detail screen. 142 - Second, the index screen _after_ adding an Americano to your cart. 143

# Digital Cafe — Overview

Source: [Alteheit/digitalcafe-2024](https://github.com/Alteheit/digitalcafe-2024), `doc/walkthrough/0001`–`0010`.

Digital Cafe is a walkthrough e-commerce app for a coffee shop: users browse products, add them to a cart, and check out. Built with Django, following the official Django tutorial flow.

## Tech stack

- **Language**: Python 3.11
- **Framework**: Django (chosen over the original Flask version because Django is more opinionated/structured)
- **Database**: SQLite (`db.sqlite3`), via Django's ORM and migrations
- **Templating**: Django Template Language (`{% %}` control tags, `{{ }}` variables), server-rendered multi-page app (no SPA/frontend framework)
- **Auth**: Django's built-in `django.contrib.auth` User model and session-based login (native username/password only — no federated/OAuth login)
- **Admin**: Django's built-in admin app (`django.contrib.admin`) for non-technical CRUD
- **Project layout**: single Django app named `core` inside a project also named `digitalcafe`, using a Python virtualenv (`env/`)

## Django apps / models

Everything lives in one app, `core`. Models are added incrementally across the walkthrough:

| Model | Fields | Added in |
|---|---|---|
| `Product` | `name` (CharField), `price` (IntegerField) | 0005 |
| `CartItem` | `user` (FK → `User`, CASCADE), `product` (FK → `Product`, CASCADE), `quantity` (IntegerField) | 0009 |
| `Transaction` | `user` (FK → `User`, CASCADE), `created_at` (DateTimeField) | 0010 |
| `LineItem` | `transaction` (FK → `Transaction`, CASCADE), `product` (FK → `Product`, CASCADE), `quantity` (IntegerField) | 0010 |

- `User` is Django's built-in auth model (`django.contrib.auth.models.User`) — no custom user model is created; the walkthrough notes that if extra fields were needed later, the recommended pattern is a one-to-one companion model.
- Each user is assumed to have one implicit "cart" (their own `CartItem` rows), not a separate `Cart` model.
- Checkout converts a user's `CartItem`s into a `Transaction` + `LineItem`s, then deletes the `CartItem`s.
- All models are registered in `core/admin.py` via `admin.site.register(...)` so superusers can manage them through `/admin`.

## Main pages / routes

All routes are registered in `core/urls.py` and included from the project's root `digitalcafe/urls.py` via `include("core.urls")`.

| Path | View | Purpose | Auth |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/` | `index` | List all products (table), greet logged-in user, show flash messages, link to checkout | `@login_required` |
| `/product/<int:product_id>` | `product_detail` | Show one product's name/price; GET renders page, POST adds a `CartItem` (quantity + hidden product_id field) | `@login_required` |
| `/accounts/login/` | `login_view` | GET renders login form; POST authenticates via `authenticate()`/`login()`, shows flash message on failure, redirects to `index` on success | public |
| `/checkout` | `checkout` | GET shows current `CartItem`s and a checkout form; POST converts them into a `Transaction` + `LineItem`s and clears the cart | `@login_required` |
| `/admin/` | Django admin | Built-in CRUD UI for `Product`, `CartItem`, `Transaction`, `LineItem`, and `User` | superuser login |

Left as an exercise (not implemented in the walkthrough): a transaction-history page for users to view past orders.

## Order of implementation (walkthrough steps 0001–0010)

1. **0001 — Digital Cafe**: intro, objectives, environment setup (Python 3.11, venv, `pip install django`).
2. **0002 — Hello Django**: `django-admin startproject digitalcafe`; understand true root / project root / package directory; run `manage.py runserver`.
3. **0003 — Your first page**: `manage.py startapp core`; first view function (`index`) returning `HttpResponse`; wire it up in `core/urls.py` and include that in the project's `urls.py`.
4. **0004 — HTML**: register `core` in `INSTALLED_APPS`; introduce templates (`core/templates/core/index.html`); render `index` via `loader.get_template` + context dict instead of hardcoded HTML strings.
5. **0005 — The database**: run `migrate` to set up SQLite; define `Product` model; `makemigrations` / `migrate` workflow; interact with models via `manage.py shell`; switch `index` to read from the database.
6. **0006 — The admin site**: `createsuperuser`; register `Product` in `core/admin.py` to enable CRUD via `/admin`.
7. **0007 — Viewing products**: add `product/<int:product_id>` route and `product_detail` view; fetch by ID from the database; link product rows from the index table; add `product_detail.html` template.
8. **0008 — Users**: protect `index`/`product_detail` with `@login_required`; build `login_view` (GET renders form, POST calls `authenticate`/`login`, flash messages on failure); register `accounts/login/` route; greet logged-in user by username.
9. **0009 — The cart**: add `CartItem` model (FK to `User` and `Product`); register with admin; add an "Add to cart" form to the product detail page; extend `product_detail` to handle POST (create `CartItem`, flash a confirmation message, redirect to index).
10. **0010 — Checkout**: add `Transaction` and `LineItem` models; add `checkout` view/route/template (GET shows cart summary, POST converts `CartItem`s into a `Transaction` + `LineItem`s and deletes the `CartItem`s); link to `/checkout` from the index page.

**General workflow pattern used throughout**: for any new feature — (1) design/update the model(s) → `makemigrations` → `migrate` → optionally register with admin; (2) write the view function; (3) register the view in `core/urls.py`; (4) if it's a new app, register the app's urls in the project's `urls.py`; (5) build the HTML template.

Build "Digital Cafe," a web app for a coffee shop where users can browse products, add them to a cart, and check out.

Tech stack: Python 3.11, Django (server-rendered, no frontend framework), SQLite as the database via Django's ORM, Django's built-in django.contrib.auth for username/password login, and Django's built-in admin app for managing data.

Data models:
- Product: name, price
- CartItem: linked to a user and a product, with a quantity
- Transaction: linked to a user, with a timestamp
- LineItem: linked to a transaction and a product, with a quantity

Pages/features:
- A home page listing all products, visible only to logged-in users, greeting the user by name
- A product detail page showing one product's name and price, with a form to add it to the cart (quantity input)
- A login page (username/password, with an error message shown on failed login)
- A checkout page showing the current cart contents, with a button to convert the cart into a completed transaction and clear the cart
- An admin panel where a superuser can manage products, cart items, transactions, and line items
- An order history page where a logged-in user can view their past transactions and what was purchased in each

There's already a study doc at doc/study/0001-digital-cafe-overview.md covering the original walkthrough's scope. Use it as your base. Following the workflow in CLAUDE.md, write a plan doc in doc/plan/ covering the full build (all models, pages, and the order history addition), then execute it on a feature branch, following Conventional Commits. Confirm each doc/plan/code file actually gets written to disk (use ls to check) before moving to the next step.

# Digital Cafe — Build Plan

Base: `doc/study/0001-digital-cafe-overview.md`. This plan covers the full target
scope — all four models, all five walkthrough pages, plus an order-history page
that the original walkthrough left as an exercise.

Branch: `feature/build-digital-cafe`. Commits follow Conventional Commits
(`feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`, `docs:`, scoped as `feat(core): ...` where useful).

## Target project layout

```
digital-cafe-vibecoded/          # repo root (== "true root")
├── doc/
├── env/                         # Python 3.11 venv, gitignored
└── digitalcafe/                 # Django project root (manage.py lives here)
    ├── manage.py
    ├── digitalcafe/             # package dir: settings.py, urls.py, wsgi.py, asgi.py
    └── core/                    # single app: models, views, urls, admin, templates
        └── templates/core/*.html
```

## Data model (final state)

- `Product`: `name` (CharField), `price` (IntegerField)
- `CartItem`: `user` (FK → `User`, CASCADE), `product` (FK → `Product`, CASCADE), `quantity` (IntegerField)
- `Transaction`: `user` (FK → `User`, CASCADE), `created_at` (DateTimeField)
- `LineItem`: `transaction` (FK → `Transaction`, CASCADE), `product` (FK → `Product`, CASCADE), `quantity` (IntegerField)

`User` is Django's built-in auth model — no custom user model.

## Routes (final state)

| Path | View | Auth | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/` | `index` | required | product list, greeting, flash messages, links to checkout + order history |
| `/product/<int:product_id>` | `product_detail` | required | GET shows product + add-to-cart form; POST creates/updates a `CartItem` |
| `/accounts/login/` | `login_view` | public | GET shows form; POST authenticates, flashes error on failure |
| `/checkout` | `checkout` | required | GET shows cart summary; POST converts cart → `Transaction` + `LineItem`s, clears cart |
| `/orders` | `order_history` | required | **new** — lists the user's past `Transaction`s, each with its `LineItem`s |
| `/admin/` | Django admin | superuser | CRUD for all four models |

## Build steps

1. **Environment & scaffolding** (`chore:`)
   - Create venv at `env/`, add `.gitignore` (venv, `__pycache__`, `db.sqlite3`, `*.pyc`).
   - `pip install django`, freeze to `digitalcafe/requirements.txt`.
   - `django-admin startproject digitalcafe`, `python manage.py startapp core`.
   - Register `core.apps.CoreConfig` in `INSTALLED_APPS`.
   - Commit: `chore: scaffold Django project and core app`

2. **Models** (`feat(core):`)
   - Add all four models to `core/models.py` in one pass (`Product`, `CartItem`, `Transaction`, `LineItem`), each with a `__str__`.
   - `makemigrations core && migrate`.
   - Commit: `feat(core): add Product, CartItem, Transaction, and LineItem models`

3. **Admin registration** (`feat(core):`)
   - Register all four models in `core/admin.py`.
   - `createsuperuser` (manual step, not committed — credentials aren't code).
   - Commit: `feat(core): register models with the admin site`

4. **Auth / login page** (`feat(core):`)
   - `login_view`: GET renders `core/login_view.html`; POST authenticates via `authenticate()`/`login()`, flashes an error message and redisplays the form on failure, redirects to `index` on success.
   - Route `accounts/login/` in `core/urls.py`; wire `core/urls.py` into the project's `urls.py` via `include`.
   - Commit: `feat(core): add login page and authentication`

5. **Home page** (`feat(core):`)
   - `index` view (`@login_required`): lists all `Product`s, greets `request.user.username`, renders flash messages.
   - `core/templates/core/index.html`.
   - Commit: `feat(core): add product listing home page`

6. **Product detail + add to cart** (`feat(core):`)
   - `product_detail` view (`@login_required`): GET shows one product; POST reads `quantity` + hidden `product_id`, creates a `CartItem` for `request.user`, flashes a confirmation, redirects to `index`.
   - Route `product/<int:product_id>`.
   - `core/templates/core/product_detail.html` with the add-to-cart form.
   - Commit: `feat(core): add product detail page with add-to-cart form`

7. **Checkout** (`feat(core):`)
   - `checkout` view (`@login_required`): GET lists the user's `CartItem`s; POST converts each into a `LineItem` under a new `Transaction` (timestamped with `datetime.now(tz=timezone.utc)`), then deletes the `CartItem`s, flashes a thank-you message, redirects to `index`.
   - Route `checkout`; `core/templates/core/checkout.html`; link from `index.html`.
   - Commit: `feat(core): add checkout page and transaction creation`

8. **Order history** (`feat(core):`) — addition beyond the original walkthrough
   - `order_history` view (`@login_required`): fetch `Transaction.objects.filter(user=request.user)` ordered newest-first, and for each transaction its `LineItem_set.all()` (product name, quantity).
   - Route `orders`; `core/templates/core/order_history.html` showing one section/table per transaction (timestamp + line items); link from `index.html`.
   - Commit: `feat(core): add order history page`

9. **Manual verification pass** (no commit, or `test:` notes if anything is added)
   - Run `python manage.py runserver`; walk the happy path: register/login → browse products → add to cart → checkout → view order history → confirm cart is empty and admin shows the new `Transaction`/`LineItem` rows.

## Out of scope

- Payment processing, inventory/stock tracking, product images, editing/removing individual cart items, quantity merging on repeat add-to-cart, password reset/registration UI, CSS/styling polish, automated test suite. These can be follow-up work but aren't part of this build.

"""
URL configuration for digitalcafe project.

The `urlpatterns` list routes URLs to views. For more information please see:
    https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/topics/http/urls/
Examples:
Function views
    1. Add an import:  from my_app import views
    2. Add a URL to urlpatterns:  path('', views.home, name='home')
Class-based views
    1. Add an import:  from other_app.views import Home
    2. Add a URL to urlpatterns:  path('', Home.as_view(), name='home')
Including another URLconf
    1. Import the include() function: from django.urls import include, path
    2. Add a URL to urlpatterns:  path('blog/', include('blog.urls'))
"""
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
]
